title: Transductive Inference for Text Classification using Support Vector Machines
venue: Proceedings of the Sixteenth International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML-99)
conclusions: Introduces Transductive Support Vector Machines (TSVMs), which jointly optimize a max-margin hyperplane over labeled training data and a labeling of a given, fixed test set (Vapnik's transductive setting) rather than inducing a general decision function.

Proves the transductive learning problem reduces to selecting among finitely many training/test equivalence classes and gives a structural-risk-minimization bound (Theorem 1) showing large-margin separation of train+test controls the effective hypothesis-space size.

Proposes a practical local-search training algorithm (label-switching + incremental slack costs C-*, C+*) that scales TSVM training to test sets of 10,000+ examples, with a proof of finite-step convergence (Theorem 2).

Empirically shows TSVMs beat inductive SVM and Naive Bayes on Reuters-21578, WebKB, and Ohsumed, with the largest gains for very small training sets and large test sets (P/R-breakeven point improves from 48.4 to 60.8 average on Reuters).

Argues text classification is well-suited to transduction because of high-dimensional, sparse, co-occurrence-structured features, letting the test set's word co-occurrence patterns inform the decision boundary.

Notes the approach can hurt performance on classes with weak within-class topic coherence (e.g. WebKB 'project' category) when too few training examples are available to rule out spurious topic generalization.
our_use: main.tex:218, in the 'Transductive and set-level constraints' related-work paragraph: 'Transductive inference reasons about a fixed unlabeled test set \citep{vapnik1998statistical,joachims1999transductive}...' -- cited alongside Vapnik as the canonical/founding example of transductive inference reasoning about a fixed, given test set, before contrasting it with TraLO's hard argmax count-budget constraint.
